There has been a lot of misinformation and lazy guesswork regarding omnibus bills, so lets get to the bottom of what an omnibus spending bill is as well as the extent that the President can re-delegate funds from them.

What the hell is an omnibus?

An omnibus spending bill is just a collection of smaller appropriation bills into a larger spending bill. There are 12 appropriation bills that are theoretically needed every year to keep the federal government funded, so an omnibus is merely when two or more appropriation bills are bundled together. Appropriation bills are a large part of the annual budgeting process of the federal government and the power of congress to make such bills comes from the Constitution (Article I, section 9, clause 7).

How does the budgeting process work?

The annual budgeting process begins with the President sending in the form of a request a proposed budget, this request has no binding authority in congress and is basically a list of preferences. Congress responds by first drafting a congressional budget resolution, aka a "302a allocation", which sets the total amount of discretionary funding for that year. Any congressional budget resolution that extends beyond a year (say a 5 year budget resolution), isn't actually binding beyond a year.

From there the budgeting process moves to the appropriation committees in each chamber. These committees are responsible for determining program-by-program funding levels, this is done through 12 distinct appropriation bills, each generated by a distinct sub-committee. These sub-committees are responsible for individual agencies or groups of agencies. The appropriations committee chairperson works with the chairs of the subcommittees to divide the 302a allocation amongst the 12 subcommittees, the allocation to any individual subcommittee is called the "302b allocation".

Now we get to the appropriation bills. Through hearings, testimonies, and other requests, each subcommittee allocates their 302b across various programs as they see fit. In appropriation bills it has become common for legislators to include policy changes (colloquially called "riders"), for example changing agency procedure to be more efficient or prohibiting an agency from spending the money on something the legislators oppose. It is these policy changes that complicate the process of getting these bills passed, as appropriation bills are supposed to pass entirely by both chambers and signed by the President, meaning they are subject to political differences and all the shenanigans we have come to expect from our system.

What happens when the appropriation bills fail to pass?

When the appropriation bills fail to pass it can result in government shutdowns. However, appropriation bills don't usually pass as intended, given our contentious political system very often we have looming shutdowns and so legislators employ stop-gap measures, called "continuing resolutions", to only temporarily fund the government for weeks or months at a time.

Now this is where omnibus spending bills come in. With so much room for disagreement and stagnation, it is very difficult to pass each appropriation bill itself and in the appropriate time. As such, when the fiscal year ends leadership in both chambers will negotiate to pass many or all of the appropriation bills at once in one combined package. Given the President's inability to line-item veto, passing them all at once drastically decreases the chance of any one bill being hamstringed in a chamber or vetoes by the President, allowing a greater range of negotiation between congressional leaders.

What about these Letters from the President I've been seeing?

In theory the budget and appropriations process is intended to encompass all federal spending. In practice bureaucratic bloat has led to many occasions where Congress passes legislation that allows for spending outside the normal budgeting process. This can mask the total amount Congress spends and usually takes the form of emergency funding. Likewise, Congress has occasionally taken additional steps to address or constrain the budget through additional legislation in the form of deficit/budget control acts. These recent letters to chamber leadership from President Trump are formal notifications that he is triggering some of these procedures.

So President Trump can now ignore the appropriation bills and spend all the money however he wants?!!

Absolutely not. Congress wouldn't just legislate away one of its most important powers, and so have very narrowly defined these procedures which the President can trigger. That however is tangential since that isn't at all the intent of President Trump's letter.

Let's take a look at one of the letters:

In accordance with section 7058(d) of division K of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2018 (H.R. 1625; the “Act”), I hereby designate as an emergency requirement all funding so designated by the Congress in the Act pursuant to section 251(b)(2)(A) of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985, for the accounts referenced in section 7058(d).

So this letter is solely about the accounts referenced in section 7058(d) of division K. Now let's take a closer look at 7058(d) of division K of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2018:

(d) REPURPOSED FUNDS .—(1) Of the unobligated balances available under the heading ‘‘Bilateral Economic Assistance’’ in title IX of the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2015 (division J of Public Law 113–235)—

(A) $35,000,000 shall be made available for the Emergency Reserve Fund...

(B) $100,000,000 shall be for programs to accelerate the capabilities of targeted countries to prevent, detect, and respond to infectious disease out-breaks; and

(C) $10,000,000 shall be made available for support of a multi-partner trust fund or other multilateral efforts to assist communities in Haiti..

We can see clearly that the accounts in question total only 145 million dollars, this is a far cry from Trump writing himself a blank check or seizing unilateral control of budget as allocated by the omnibus spending bill. In short, this letter from the President isn't at all what some have tried to make it out to be.

Okay, what kind of things were designated as part of this appropriations budget?

The budget was for over a trillion dollars, so a lot of money has been allocated. Now to address some of the bizarre rumors being propagated around voat:

"Obama created omnibus spending bills"

False. Congress puts together omnibus spending bills and this precedes the Obama administration entirely. For example the omnibus bills of '05, '93' and '90.

"Obama used omnibus to avoid having a budget"

False. Aside from the fact that congressional leaders put together appropriation bills, whether separately or packaged together as an omnibus, an omnibus spending bill IS the budget, it is no more or less a budget than any other appropriation bill, which are essential parts of the annual budget.

"Trump is under no obligation to fund the projects in the appropriation bills"

The legislative branch holds the purse strings and it funds the projects. The executive branch executes the will of congress, the range of discretion the executive branch has in spending is narrowly outlined by congress.

"The omnibus is nothing like a budget because it is discretionary spending"

This is a misunderstanding of the term "discretionary spending" insofar as it applies to federal funding. Federal funding can be split into a few broad categories including federal student loans, interest on the debt, mandatory spending, and discretionary spending. Mandatory programs are programs that are funded automatically by law regardless of their annual cost to the treasury. Discretionary spending on the other hand is explicitly the budget as allocated by annual appropriation bills.
